title: Explain Concepts Related to Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) Pipelines

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: A continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipeline automates the journey from code change to tested, packaged, and potentially deployed software.
Instead of developers manually performing every step, the pipeline creates a repeatable workflow.
The basic mental model is: code → integrate → build → test → secure → package → deploy.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Where is the software in the pipeline: integrating code, building it, testing it, packaging it, or deploying it?
sections.callout: An automated code-to-deployment process → CI/CD pipeline.

sections.title: Automation
paragraphs: Automation removes repetitive manual work from the software delivery process.
A pipeline may start when code changes, build software, run tests, perform security checks, create artifacts, and deploy applications.
Think: A developer changes code; the pipeline starts doing the chores.
sections.callout: Repetitive development or deployment steps happen automatically → automation.

sections.title: Code Integration
paragraphs: Continuous integration frequently combines developer changes into the shared codebase and validates those changes.
It reduces problems caused when developers work separately for long periods and then try to combine huge changes at once.
Think: Integrate small changes often.
sections.callout: Developer code is frequently combined and automatically validated → code integration.

sections.title: Code Deployment
paragraphs: Code deployment moves software into an environment where it can run.
A CI/CD pipeline can automate deployment after code successfully passes required stages.
Think: Get the tested software into the destination environment.
sections.callout: Approved code is automatically released into an environment → deployment.

sections.title: Build
paragraphs: The build stage converts source code into a form that can be executed or packaged.
Depending on the application, this may involve compiling code, resolving dependencies, packaging files, or creating an image.
Think: Turn source code into something deployable.
sections.callout: Source code is being converted into a usable software artifact → build.

sections.title: Testing
paragraphs: Automated testing checks whether software behaves as expected and can catch problems before deployment.
Think: Does the new code actually work?
sections.callout: The pipeline automatically validates application behavior → testing.

sections.title: Security
paragraphs: Security checks can be integrated into the pipeline instead of waiting until after deployment.
The goal is to identify security problems earlier in the delivery process.
Think: Security is part of the pipeline, not an afterthought.
sections.callout: Code or artifacts are checked for security weaknesses during CI/CD → pipeline security.

sections.title: Workflow
paragraphs: A workflow defines the sequence of pipeline activities.
For example: Commit → Build → Test → Security Check → Package → Deploy.
Think: What happens first, second, third, and next?
sections.callout: The scenario describes ordered CI/CD stages → workflow.

sections.title: Artifacts
paragraphs: An artifact is an output produced by the pipeline that can be stored, distributed, or deployed.
CompTIA specifically lists images, packages, and flat files.

entries.title: Images: VM Image
paragraphs: A virtual machine (VM) image is a prepared representation used to create virtual machines. Think: Template for a VM.
entries.recognitionCue: The pipeline produces something used to launch identical virtual machines → VM image.

entries.title: Images: Container Image
paragraphs: A container image packages application code and required components used to launch containers. Think: Container blueprint.
entries.recognitionCue: The artifact is used to start containers → container image.

entries.title: Packages: Red Hat Package Manager (RPM)
paragraphs: RPM packages software commonly associated with Red Hat-family Linux systems.

entries.title: Packages: Debian
paragraphs: Debian-based environments use Debian package formats for software installation.

entries.title: Packages: ZIP
paragraphs: A ZIP file bundles and compresses files into one archive. Think: Pack several files together.
entries.recognitionCue: Files are bundled into a common compressed archive → ZIP.

entries.title: Packages: tar
paragraphs: A tar archive bundles multiple files together and is common in Unix and Linux environments.
entries.recognitionCue: Unix or Linux files are collected into a tar archive → tar.

entries.title: Flat File
paragraphs: A flat file is a simple file containing information without the richer structure of a database.
Pipeline output can be stored as a flat file when a simple format is sufficient.
entries.recognitionCue: The artifact is an individual data or configuration file → flat file.

sections.title: Repositories
paragraphs: Repositories store code, packages, images, or other artifacts.

entries.title: Public Repository
paragraphs: A public repository is broadly accessible according to its permissions and is commonly used to distribute software or artifacts to many users.
entries.recognitionCue: Software or artifacts must be broadly accessible → public repository.

entries.title: Private Repository
paragraphs: A private repository restricts access to authorized users or systems. Organizations may use it for proprietary code or internal artifacts.
Think: Company-only warehouse.
entries.recognitionCue: Code or artifacts should only be accessible internally or to authorized users → private repository.

sections.title: CI/CD Recognition Flow
paragraphs: Developer commits → Code integrates → Build → Testing → Security checks → Artifact created → Artifact stored in a repository → Deployment.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Frequently combine developer changes → Code integration
Release approved code into an environment → Code deployment
Turn source into deployable output → Build
Check for vulnerabilities during the pipeline → Security

entries.title: Continuous Integration vs. Deployment
paragraphs: Integration combines and validates code. Deployment releases it into an environment. Code entering the shared branch does not automatically mean it has been deployed.

entries.title: Build vs. Artifact
paragraphs: Build is the process. An artifact is the output of that process.

entries.title: Container Image vs. Running Container
paragraphs: The image is the reusable artifact. The container is the running workload created from it.

entries.title: Public vs. Private Repository
paragraphs: The difference is primarily access. Internal proprietary artifacts belong in appropriately restricted repositories.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Combine developer changes frequently → Continuous integration
Convert source code into deployable form → Build
Check software security during pipeline → Security
Virtual machine deployment template → VM image
